title: Number Bases
learning_objectives: Read a numeral in any base by its place values and explain why the base decides the digit set.
Convert a numeral from another base to base 10 by expanding it in powers of its base.
Convert a base 10 numeral to another base by repeated division, reading the remainders in reverse order.
Add and subtract numerals in another base, carrying and borrowing in that base.
Build and use the addition and multiplication tables of a base.
Multiply numerals in another base and divide by reversing the multiplication table.
Detect an illegal digit or a lost digit as evidence of a conversion or arithmetic error.

sections.title: Place value and the digits of a base
sections.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Another Base into Base 10 and Other Bases', from the introduction through the counting examples
objectives: Explain how place value turns a string of digits into a quantity in any base.
List the legal digits of a base, using capital letters for values above 9.
Write the counting sequence of a base up to $100_b$.

misconceptions.correction: $10_b$ means the base itself: $10_2 = 2$, $10_6 = 6$ and $10_{12} = 12$. The numeral 10 means ten only in base 10.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Another Base into Base 10 and Other Bases'

misconceptions.claim: A digit may take any value from 0 to 9 in any base.
misconceptions.correction: A base $b$ has exactly $b$ digits, 0 to $b-1$. Base 6 has no 6, 7, 8 or 9, and base 14 continues with A, B, C and D after 9.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Another Base into Base 10 and Other Bases'

summary: In base $b$, each place is worth a power of $b$: ones, $b$, $b^2$, and so on.
A base $b$ uses exactly the digits 0 to $b-1$, with A, B, C and so on standing for 10, 11, 12 and so on.
Counting to $100_b$ means using every digit in the leading place once, then starting a third place.

hints: Start from 0 and change the leading digit only after the ones place has used every symbol.
The base 14 digits run 0 to 9, then A, B, C and D.
Base 2 has only two symbols, so the sequence is short.

sections.title: From another base to base 10
sections.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Another Base into Base 10 and Other Bases', conversion examples
objectives: Expand a numeral in base $b$ as a sum of digits times powers of $b$.
Evaluate a base $b$ numeral in base 10, including numerals that use letters as digits.

misconceptions.claim: The digits of a base $b$ numeral are added together, then multiplied by the base.
misconceptions.correction: Each digit is multiplied by its own power of the base, and the products are added: $3,601_7 = 3(7^3) + 6(7^2) + 0(7) + 1$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Another Base into Base 10 and Other Bases'

misconceptions.claim: A letter digit has no value in arithmetic.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Another Base into Base 10 and Other Bases'

summary: Write the numeral with its powers of the base, starting from the rightmost digit as $b^0$.
Replace each letter by its value before calculating.
The result is an ordinary base 10 number, so it takes no subscript.

hints: The four digits occupy the powers $7^3$, $7^2$, $7^1$ and $7^0$.
Replace B by 11 before you multiply by the powers of 14.
Replace A by 10 before you multiply by the powers of 12.
The powers of 2 run 8, 4, 2 and 1 from left to right in a four-digit numeral.

sections.title: From base 10 to another base
sections.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Base 10 into Another Base'
objectives: Convert a base 10 number to a lower or higher base by repeated division.
Read the remainders in reverse order and write any value above 9 as a letter.

misconceptions.claim: The remainders are read from top to bottom.
misconceptions.correction: The last remainder is the leading digit. For 298, the remainders 4, 1, 2 and 1 give $1214_6$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Base 10 into Another Base'

misconceptions.claim: A remainder of 11 can be written as 11 in base 13.
misconceptions.correction: Every digit must be below the base, so 11 is written B in base 13. The conversion of 45,134 ends with the digits 1, 7, 7, 0 and B.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Conversion of Base 10 into Another Base'

summary: Divide by the target base, keep the remainder, and continue with the quotient.
Stop when the quotient is 0.
Read the remainders from the last one to the first, and write values above 9 as letters.

hints: Divide 298 by 6, then divide each quotient by 6 until the quotient is 0.
The remainders include 11, which is written B in base 13.
Keep dividing by 2 until the quotient reaches 0, then reverse the remainders.

sections.title: Checking a conversion for errors
sections.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Errors in Converting Between Bases'
objectives: Detect an illegal digit in a numeral written in another base.
Use the number of digits to test whether a conversion could be right.

misconceptions.claim: A numeral is valid as long as the arithmetic looks right.
misconceptions.correction: A numeral in base $b$ cannot contain a digit $b$ or larger. $2081_7$ is wrong on sight because 8 is not a base 7 digit.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Errors in Converting Between Bases'

misconceptions.claim: Converting to a smaller base can shorten the numeral.
misconceptions.correction: A smaller base needs at least as many digits. A five-digit base 10 number cannot become a four-digit base 5 number.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00054, section 'Errors in Converting Between Bases'

summary: Check the digit set first: every digit must be less than the base.
A remainder at or above the base is an illegal digit.
Converting to a smaller base cannot reduce the number of digits, and converting to a larger base cannot increase it.

sections.title: Adding in another base
sections.locator: CNXML module m00055, section 'Addition in Bases Other Than Base 10'
objectives: Build the addition table of a base.
Add numerals in another base, carrying a group of the base to the next place.

misconceptions.claim: Addition in another base follows the base 10 addition facts.
misconceptions.correction: The facts change with the base. In base 6, $5 + 3 = 12_6$, because five plus three is eight, and eight is one group of six and two ones.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00055, section 'Addition in Bases Other Than Base 10'

misconceptions.correction: A carry is one group of the base, so it is written 10 in that base, not ten. In base 2, $1 + 1 = 10_2$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00055, section 'Addition in Bases Other Than Base 10'

summary: Build the addition table first; the diagonal after the filled cells is where the base is written as 10.
Add column by column from the right, exactly as in base 10.
When a column reaches the base, write the remainder and carry one to the next place.

hints: The ones digits add to 4, then the sixes digits add to $12_6$.
Fill the legal sums first, then put 10 one place past the last filled cell.
Base 12 runs 0 to 9, then A and B. The entry after B is 10.
Add the ones column first and carry whenever the sum reaches 12.
In base 2, $1 + 1 = 10_2$, so carry as soon as a column reaches 2.

sections.title: Subtracting in another base
sections.locator: CNXML module m00055, sections 'Subtraction in Bases Other Than Base 10' and 'Errors When Adding and Subtracting in Bases Other Than Base 10'
objectives: Subtract numerals in another base, borrowing one group of the base when needed.
Explain whether an error in a base arithmetic statement comes from an illegal digit or a base 10 fact.

misconceptions.claim: Borrowing adds ten to the column.
misconceptions.correction: Borrowing adds one group of the base. In base 6, borrowing adds 6, so $12_6 - 4_6 = 4_6$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00055, section 'Subtraction in Bases Other Than Base 10'

misconceptions.correction: Nine plus six is fifteen, which is one group of twelve and three ones, so $9_{12} + 6_{12} = 13_{12}$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00055, section 'Errors When Adding and Subtracting in Bases Other Than Base 10'

summary: Borrow one group of the base from the next place when the top digit is smaller.
Use the addition table backwards to find each difference.
Check every digit against the base, and check every sum against the base's addition table.

hints: Borrowing from the sixes place turns the 2 into $12_6$.
Borrow from A to make the middle digit $11_{12}$.
Work out $9 + 6$ in base 12 before you compare the answer with the written one.

sections.title: Multiplying and dividing in another base
sections.locator: CNXML module m00056, sections 'Multiplication in Bases Other Than 10', 'Division in Bases Other Than 10' and their errors section
objectives: Build the multiplication table of a base from its addition table.
Multiply numerals in another base, carrying in that base and adding the partial products in that base.
Divide in another base by reversing the multiplication table.
Recognise an illegal digit or a base 10 product as an error.

misconceptions.claim: A multiplication table is the same in every base.
misconceptions.correction: The entries change with the base. In base 6, $4 \times 5 = 32_6$, not 20.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00056, section 'Multiplication in Bases Other Than 10'

misconceptions.claim: The base 10 product is the answer in any base.
misconceptions.correction: In base 12, $8 \times 7$ is 56 in base 10, which is $48_{12}$: four twelves and eight ones.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m00056, section 'Errors in Multiplying and Dividing in Bases Other Than Base 10'

summary: Multiplication is repeated addition, so build its table from the addition table.
Multiply as in base 10, but take every digit and every carry from the base's tables.
Division asks which factor in the multiplication table gives the dividend.
A digit at or above the base, or a base 10 fact used unchanged, is an error.

hints: Build the base 7 table by repeated addition, using the base 7 addition table.
The entry $7 \times 9$ is $53_{12}$; use it to check your table.
Multiply by 4 first, then by 7, and add the two rows in base 12.
Work out $8 \times 7$ in base 12 before you compare the answer with the written one.

exam_recall_checks.subject: mathematics
exam_recall_checks.stem: What is the value of $10_6$ in base 10?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: In base 6 the second place is worth 6, so $10_6 = 1 \times 6 + 0 = 6$.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB mathematics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: mathematics
exam_recall_checks.stem: Which set gives the digits used in base 9?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: A base 9 system has exactly nine symbols, 0 to 8. The symbol 9 is not legal in base 9.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB mathematics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: general-mathematics
exam_recall_checks.stem: Which list gives the first four numerals after $3_4$ in base 4?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Base 4 has the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3. Once 3 is used, the next numeral is $10_4$, then $11_4$, $12_4$ and $13_4$. The digit 4 is not legal in base 4.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC general-mathematics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: mathematics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A base 10 number is converted to base 8 and the result is $27A_8$. What is wrong with the result?

options.text: A is not a legal base 8 digit
7 is not a legal base 8 digit
The numeral has too few digits

exam_recall_checks.explanation: Base 8 uses only 0 to 7. The letter A stands for 10, which is at or above the base, so the numeral cannot be valid.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB mathematics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: general-mathematics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A four-digit base 10 number is converted to base 7 and the result has three digits. What does this show?

options.text: The result is correct because 7 is smaller than 10
The result is correct because 7 is larger than 3

exam_recall_checks.explanation: A smaller base needs at least as many digits, so a four-digit number cannot become a three-digit number when it is converted to base 7.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC general-mathematics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: mathematics
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The ones column gives $6 + 5 = 11 = 14_7$, so write 4 and carry 1. The sevens column gives $1 + 4 + 2 = 7 = 10_7$, so write 0 and carry 1. The answer is $104_7$.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB mathematics syllabus
